name: r8-m10
statement: Each trained model's within-problem precision falls with answer length only beyond the length its training let it run: Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math, trained at a 16k completion budget with truncated rollouts scored as failures, learned to commit before the cap, so its answers past about 8,000 tokens are mostly unsupported finishes, while Think-SFT, imitating long teacher traces, keeps working (or runs into the cap) and holds its precision to 16,384 tokens; hence the Think-SFT-over-RL lead sits only in long answers and grows with the token cap.
scope: Covers allenai/Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math (plain) against allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Think-SFT (cue), and Think-SFT + a(RL - base) transplants, on hard328, MATH-500 and fresh2026 at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, grader v3, caps 16,384 and 32,768. It explains where along answer length the two models differ, not why RL beats the untrained base: it says nothing about the base's own length curve (the base was never trained on traces), loops at T 0.6, the opening cue, Code-RL or the weight-direction edits. One board item fits only partly (result-bce075, listed in conflicts).

imports.finding: Accuracy follows an inverted U in CoT length; the optimum length rises with problem difficulty and differs by model.
imports.how: Gives the form: each model has a length past which its accuracy falls, and the models differ in where that point sits. Training sets the point: RL's falls well before 16k, Think-SFT's is past 16k.

imports.finding: Scoring truncated rollouts as wrong adds reward noise and punishes sound long reasoning for its length.
imports.how: Gives the cause of RL's early drop. Olmo 3.1 trains truncated sequences as negatives at 16k, so an answer still working near the cap gets the same reward as a wrong one, and committing to some answer before the cap is never worse. On problems RL cannot solve, its long answers therefore end in asserted numbers instead of cap hits.

explains.quote: an RL answer over 8,000 tokens is right 12.5 points less often
explains.how: On the same problem RL loses precision past its learned commit length, while Think-SFT's +1.2 shows no drop up to 16k.

explains.quote: Finished answers over 12,000 tokens: right 68.2 % Think-SFT (135/198), 24.4 % RL (87/356)
explains.how: RL's answers past 12k mostly finish on problems it has not solved; Think-SFT finishes long only when it has derived the answer.

explains.quote: level with RL stopped at the same length (+0.1 [-2.2, 2.4])
explains.how: Below about 14k both models are before their drop points, so they are level. The whole lead lies in tokens past 14,028.

explains.quote: RL finishing long and wrong more often (381 samples against 281)
explains.how: The commit-before-cap policy turns would-be cap hits into long finished wrong answers.

explains.quote: RL's asserted long answers are right 17.0 % [9.0, 25.6] of the time
explains.how: The long finishes RL forces are mostly asserted, not derived, which is the unsupported-finish part of the mechanism.

explains.quote: Think-SFT abstains instead of answering wrong: 29 % cap hits on the 328
explains.how: Think-SFT's imitation policy keeps reasoning instead of committing, so its failures show up as cap hits and its long finished answers stay precise.
Adding the RL difference to Think-SFT brings in RL's commit policy: fewer cap hits, more unsupported finishes, lower precision among finished answers.

conflicts.quote: Think-SFT writes the first 50 % and RL-Zero-Math finishes: 209/328
conflicts.how: The mechanism expects RL, as finisher of long Think-SFT prefixes, to commit early and lose several problems against Think finishing its own prefix. The measured -0.6 [-4.3, +3.0] is nearly level, though the interval allows a loss of a few problems.

rival: One difficulty axis plus abstention (r6-account-rival with a selection reading): Think-SFT is simply the stronger solver on hard problems, long answers belong to hard problems, and Think-SFT's high long-answer precision comes only from cap hits removing its failures from the finished pool. RL's length has no effect of its own. The rival predicts the same within-problem long-minus-short contrast for both models (Think-SFT minus RL about 0) and no gain for Think-SFT from a larger cap beyond its general strength. The mechanism predicts a clearly positive within-problem difference, and a cap-32k gain for Think-SFT much larger than for RL.

predictions.experiment: Mechanism test, within-problem length contrast on hard328. For each model, the mean over problems of (precision of the model's finished answers of 12,000+ tokens) minus (precision of its finished answers under 8,000 tokens), taking only problems that have both kinds. Statistic = Think-SFT's mean minus RL's. The one-axis/abstention rival (difficulty alone, no length effect within a problem) predicts about 0.00. This mechanism predicts clearly positive.
predictions.recipe: Files: T = studies/rlneurons/results/thinkvote/hard328_sft1_cue_s4-01/rows.jsonl (Think-SFT cue) and R = studies/rlneurons/results/day1_3/hard328_rl_plain_s4r2-01/rows.jsonl (RL plain). In each file keep rows with attempt == 0 (a missing attempt field counts as 0), then for each (problem_index, sample) the first row in file order. Finished = cap_hit not true and finish_reason != 'length'. Cap hits are excluded entirely. Right = score_v3 == 1; a finished row with null or missing score_v3 counts as wrong. Per model and problem: S = finished rows with n_new < 8000, L = finished rows with n_new >= 12000. Keep problems with at least one S row and at least one L row. d = (right rows in L / rows in L) - (right rows in S / rows in S). M_model = arithmetic mean of d over that model's kept problems (each model has its own problem set). Statistic = M_T - M_R. If either model has fewer than 5 kept problems, the prediction counts as refuted.
predictions.refuted_by: statistic below 0.02, or fewer than 5 kept problems for either model

predictions.experiment: The same lead on short problems: on MATH-500, precision of finished answers of 8,000+ tokens, Think-SFT cue minus RL plain (4 samples each, attempt 0). The board saw no lead at any coverage on MATH-500. This mechanism puts the lead wherever an answer runs long, even on MATH-500.
predictions.recipe: Files: studies/rlneurons/results/thinkvote/math500_sft1_cue_s4-01/rows.jsonl (Think-SFT cue) and studies/rlneurons/results/day1_3/math500_rl-01/rows.jsonl (RL plain). In each file keep rows with attempt == 0 (a missing attempt counts as 0), then the first row per (problem_index, sample) in file order. Keep finished rows (cap_hit not true and finish_reason != 'length') with n_new >= 8000. Right = score_v3 == 1 (null or missing counts as wrong). Precision per model = right kept rows / kept rows. Statistic = precision(Think-SFT) - precision(RL). If either model has fewer than 20 kept rows, the prediction counts as refuted.
predictions.refuted_by: statistic below 0.0, or fewer than 20 kept rows for either model

predictions.experiment: Where the effect should not appear: on hard328, precision of finished answers under 4,000 tokens, Think-SFT cue minus RL plain. Both models are before their drop points here, so the mechanism predicts about 0.
predictions.recipe: Files T and R as in the first recipe (thinkvote/hard328_sft1_cue_s4-01/rows.jsonl and day1_3/hard328_rl_plain_s4r2-01/rows.jsonl). attempt == 0 (missing counts as 0), first row per (problem_index, sample). Keep finished rows (cap_hit not true and finish_reason != 'length') with n_new < 4000. Right = score_v3 == 1 (null or missing = wrong). Statistic = (right / kept) for T minus (right / kept) for R.

predictions.experiment: Think-SFT holds precision up to the cap: on hard328, the precision of Think-SFT cue's finished answers of 14,000 to 16,383 tokens. An error-accumulation reading (precision keeps falling with length) puts it well under its 68 % for 12k+ answers. This mechanism keeps it near that level.
predictions.recipe: File: studies/rlneurons/results/thinkvote/hard328_sft1_cue_s4-01/rows.jsonl. Rows with attempt == 0 (missing counts as 0), first row per (problem_index, sample) in file order. Keep finished rows (cap_hit not true and finish_reason != 'length') with 14000 <= n_new <= 16383. Statistic = (rows with score_v3 == 1) / (kept rows); null or missing score_v3 counts as wrong. If fewer than 20 rows are kept, the prediction counts as refuted.
predictions.refuted_by: statistic below 0.42, or fewer than 20 kept rows

predictions.experiment: RL-Zero-Math 3.1 plain on hard328 with the token cap raised to 32,768: T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, one sample, seed 3000000 (seed + index), grader v3, cap hits counted wrong. RL already commits before 16k, so the larger cap buys almost nothing (16k reference 206-207).
predictions.refuted_by: 218 or more right of 328 (RL gains from the larger cap as a still-working model would)

forecasts.reason: Think-SFT's precision holds past 16k, so many of its 29 % cap hits finish right at 32k; the vote rises from 241 by about 10.
The same text cut at 16,384 reproduces the stored 16k vote (241) up to seed noise.
Fresh contest problems demand long answers; the 32k cap adds about 7 to Think-SFT's 16k vote.
At 16k, Think-SFT's vote over 4 is about its single-sample mean (60) plus the usual vote gain.
The RL difference converts cap hits into finishes (cap hits 94 to 54), so the vote gains less than Think-SFT's +32: singles 231.5 plus about 17.
MATH-500 answers are mostly short, before both drop points, so a = 2 is about level with a = 1 (467).
As on hard328, the RL difference trades Think-SFT's cap hits for finishes, a net gain of a few problems over 60.0.
Single-sample mean of about 65 plus a vote gain smaller than Think-SFT's, because fewer cap hits leave more wrong answers that agree.

no_intervention: The mechanism is about the length policies that training installs in RL-Zero-Math and Think-SFT. The untrained base has no training-trace length to shift, and its long answers already fail to solve (result-51fd20: forced or longer budgets add nothing). So the mechanism implies no prompt, sampling, decoding or selection change to the base.
